title: Unifying Themes of Life Science

competencies.text: Explain how life forms operate as systems of related parts. Create a diagram showing structure-function relationships in biological systems.

days.title: What All Living Things Share
days.content:
🎯 Learning Target

This week you will explain how living things operate as systems of related parts and create a diagram showing structure–function relationships.

🌱 Unifying Themes

Living things are amazingly diverse — from bacteria to narra trees to tamaraw — yet they share a few big ideas:

ThemeMeaningExample
CellsAll life is made of one or more cellsBacteria (1 cell); humans (trillions)
Structure and functionA part's shape fits its jobThin, wide leaves catch light
SystemsParts interact to do more togetherHeart, vessels and blood
HomeostasisKeeping internal conditions stableSweating to cool down
EnergyLife needs a steady energy supplyPlants use light; animals eat food
HeredityDNA passes traits to offspringChildren resemble parents
InterdependenceOrganisms depend on each otherBees and flowers

🔍 Is It Alive?

To decide, check several characteristics together: made of cells, uses energy, grows, responds to stimuli, reproduces, maintains homeostasis. Fire grows and uses oxygen, but it has no cells and no DNA — so it is not alive.

✅ Quick Check

3 questions — read each explanation.

scenario.text: Fire can grow, spread and use oxygen. Why is it NOT considered a living thing?

choices.label: It has no cells and no DNA
It cannot move from place to place
It needs too much energy to stay alive
It produces carbon dioxide instead of oxygen

scenario.explanation: Living things are made of cells and pass on DNA. Fire shows some life-like behavior but lacks these basic features.

scenario.text: You shiver when you are cold. Which theme of life does this show?

choices.label: Homeostasis
Heredity and DNA
Interdependence
Evolution

scenario.explanation: Shivering produces heat to keep body temperature stable — maintaining a stable internal environment.

scenario.text: Which is the basic unit of structure and function in all living things?

choices.label: The cell
The organ
The tissue
The organism

scenario.explanation: Cell theory states that all living things are made of cells, the smallest unit that can carry out life processes.

days.title: Levels of Organization and Structure–Function
days.content:
🧱 Levels of Organization

Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ system → Organism

  • Cell: muscle cell
  • Tissue: many muscle cells working together (cardiac muscle)
  • Organ: different tissues forming one structure (the heart)
  • Organ system: organs working together (circulatory system)
  • Organism: all systems together (a person)

Each level has abilities that the levels below cannot do alone — a single heart cell cannot pump blood around the body.

🔑 Structure Fits Function

StructureFeatureFunction it supports
Red blood cellBiconcave disc, no nucleusMore room for hemoglobin; squeezes through capillaries
AlveoliMillions of tiny, thin sacsHuge surface area for gas exchange
Root hairsLong, thin extensionsMore surface to absorb water
Nerve cellLong branchesCarries signals over long distances
Small intestineVilli (finger-like folds)More area to absorb nutrients

🔗 Activity 1 — Match the Pairs

Match each structure or idea to its function or meaning. You need 70%; retakes are unlimited.

match.right: Holds more hemoglobin and fits through capillaries
match.why: Its biconcave disc shape helps it carry oxygen.

match.right: Huge surface area for gas exchange
match.why: Millions of tiny sacs let oxygen enter blood quickly.

match.right: More surface to absorb water and minerals
match.why: Thin extensions reach into soil spaces.

match.right: More area to absorb digested food

match.why: Long extensions connect distant body parts.

match.right: Group of similar cells doing one job

match.why: Example: the heart or the stomach.

match.right: Organs working together for a major task

days.title: Organisms as Systems
days.content:
🔗 Systems Depend on Each Other

No organ system works alone. When you run:

  • The muscular system needs more ATP.
  • The respiratory system brings in more oxygen; the circulatory system pumps it faster.
  • The digestive system supplied the glucose earlier.
  • The nervous system coordinates everything; the excretory and skin remove wastes and heat.

⚠️ When One Part Fails

Because systems are linked, damage to one part affects others. In emphysema, alveoli are destroyed, reducing surface area — less oxygen reaches the blood, so the heart works harder and muscles tire quickly. In diabetes, cells cannot take in glucose properly, affecting energy, eyes, kidneys and nerves.

🌳 Plants Are Systems Too

Roots absorb water and minerals; stems transport them; leaves make food and send it back down. Damage the roots and the leaves wilt; remove the leaves and the roots starve.

🎯 Activity 2 — Scenario Challenge

Reason about systems and structure–function. Read every explanation. You need 70%; retakes are unlimited.

scenario.text: A long-time smoker develops emphysema, which destroys many alveoli. Why does he get tired easily?

choices.label: Less surface area means less oxygen enters the blood
His heart starts pumping much less blood than normal
His muscles stop needing oxygen for respiration
His lungs make extra alveoli that block the airway

scenario.explanation: Fewer alveoli means less area for gas exchange, so less oxygen reaches cells for respiration — leaving him tired.

scenario.text: A plant's roots are damaged by flooding. A few days later its leaves wilt. What BEST explains this?

choices.label: Damaged roots cannot absorb enough water
Flood water fills the leaves and bursts them
Leaves stop photosynthesis to save the roots
Water in the soil turns the leaves into roots

scenario.explanation: Roots and leaves are parts of one system. Without water uptake, leaves lose turgor and wilt.

scenario.text: Which example shows the HIGHEST level of organization?

choices.label: A carabao grazing in a field
Its heart pumping blood
Its muscle tissue contracting
One cell dividing in its skin

scenario.explanation: The whole organism is above organs, tissues and cells in the levels of organization.

scenario.text: Why do cells in the small intestine have villi but cells in the skin's outer layer do not?

choices.label: Intestine cells absorb food; skin cells protect
Skin cells absorb more food than intestine cells
Villi help skin keep water out of the body
Both cells have the same job in the body

scenario.explanation: Structure matches function: villi increase absorbing area in the intestine; skin's flat, tough cells protect.

scenario.text: During a long run, which pair of systems works MOST closely to deliver oxygen to muscles?

choices.label: Respiratory and circulatory
Digestive and excretory
Skeletal and reproductive
Endocrine and integumentary

scenario.explanation: The respiratory system brings oxygen into the blood, and the circulatory system carries it to the muscles.

days.title: Diagramming Structure and Function
days.content:
🖊️ How to Make a Structure–Function Diagram

  1. Choose a system — e.g., the respiratory system or a leaf.
  2. Draw and label the parts in order (nose → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli).
  3. Beside each part, note one structural feature (cilia, C-shaped cartilage rings, thin walls).
  4. Link each feature to its function with an arrow (cartilage rings keep the trachea open).
  5. Show connections to other systems (alveoli ↔ capillaries of the circulatory system).

🧠 Sample Entries

PartStructureFunction
TracheaC-shaped cartilage ringsKeeps the airway open
Airway liningCilia and mucusTraps and sweeps out dust and germs
Alveoli wallsOne cell thick, moistFast diffusion of O₂ and CO₂
LeafFlat and wide; stomata underneathCatches light; exchanges gases

🔐 Formative Check — Escape the Lab

3 lives, 6 keys. You need 70% (5 of 6). Read each explanation.

escape.text: Which list shows levels of organization from SIMPLEST to most complex?

choices.label: Cell → tissue → organ → organ system
Organ → cell → tissue → organ system
Tissue → cell → organ system → organ
Organ system → organ → tissue → cell

escape.explanation: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs form organ systems.

escape.text: Why are alveoli walls only one cell thick?

choices.label: Gases can diffuse across them quickly
They need to be strong to hold air
They stop germs from entering blood
They make the lungs heavier and stable

escape.explanation: A very thin wall means a short distance for oxygen and carbon dioxide to diffuse between air and blood.

escape.text: What is the function of cilia in the airway?

choices.label: Sweep mucus, dust and germs out
Exchange oxygen with the blood
Pump air into the lungs directly
Produce hormones for breathing

escape.explanation: Cilia beat together to move mucus — with trapped particles — up and out of the airway.

escape.text: A leaf is flat and wide. Which function does this structure support?

choices.label: Capturing as much sunlight as possible
Storing water deep underground
Anchoring the whole plant firmly in the soil
Carrying sugar down to the roots

escape.explanation: A large, flat surface exposes more chloroplasts to light for photosynthesis.

escape.text: Bees pollinate flowers while collecting nectar. Which theme does this show?

choices.label: Interdependence
Homeostasis
Heredity and DNA
Cell theory of life

escape.explanation: Bees and flowers benefit each other — organisms depend on one another.

escape.text: A student's diagram links "alveoli" to "capillaries." Why is this link important?

choices.label: It shows two systems working together for gas exchange
It shows that alveoli are a part of the digestive system
It shows that capillaries make all the oxygen we breathe
It shows that lungs and heart are actually the same organ

escape.explanation: Oxygen passes from alveoli (respiratory) into capillaries (circulatory) — systems interact to supply cells.
